We derive the exact mean and variance of entropy under the valid-STL (VSTL) distribution, which assigns equal probability to every admissible sequence of triangle records, and provide second-order expansions that keep the global reference values practical to compute at large ?le sizes. Using these expansions, we establish a two-sided hypothesis test for the global entropy statistic, whose limiting value is lowered from 8 to 7.99991479609 bits. The format constraints also change the local entropy reference: applying the capacity energy criterion to triangle records selects a block size of 1950 bytes instead of 1936 bytes, with an exact reference mean of 7.903106732975 rather than 7.902469316647 bits. Although small, these shifts are su?cient to place the VSTL reference means outside the conventional 95% acceptance intervals at practical ?le sizes, making unadjusted entropy tests prone to falsely rejecting ideal VSTL ciphertexts. Monte-Carlo simulations con?rm all reference values within sampling error. We therefore recommend using the format-speci?c reference values derived here to evaluate STL ciphers.

cs.CR / 26 / 2610.20567
Prioritizing Microservice Requests via Retries
Ofek Lavi, Jhonatan Tavori, Hanoch Levy, Anat Bremler-Barr
cs.NI · cs.CR · cs.DC
Abstract
Cloud services rapidly shift towards independently-managed microservices architectures. This independence may lead to temporary microservices miscoordination, resulting in overloads and rejections of valuable transactions. This weakness may further be exploited by attackers to launch overload attacks inflicting performance and cost damages. Retry operations are a key machinery aiming at overcoming seldom rejections. However, during overload periods they: a) Fail protecting valuable transactions from rejections, and b) Trigger large-scale performance-degrading retry storms. We propose simple modifications in retry operations, overcoming these deficiencies by transforming retries into a rejection prioritization mechanism, DiffTry (Differential Retries). It is based on a simple, lightweight, distributed and stateless design and requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination. We develop an analytical model capturing DiffTry's effectiveness for two services in tandem, then generalize it to networks of services. Our theoretical framework lets practitioners quantify, for a given network, the resulting prioritization and rejection rates, and yields formal guarantees that DiffTry substantially reduces the impact of both incidental and adversarial orchestrated overloads. We validate these predictions in simulation and on a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry is a simple drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application changes; the measured rejection closely matches the analysis.

cs.CR / 27 / 2610.20537
Quantum-Aware Key Rank for Side-Channel Attacks evaluation
Yevgen Kotukh
quant-ph · cs.CR
Abstract
Side-channel attacks on block ciphers rarely recover the key outright: they leave a residual key space ordered by subkey posteriors, and evaluation laboratories report the key rank of the true key against thresholds near 2^48 and 2^60. No evaluation framework models an adversary who collects traces classically and finishes the search on a quantum computer, although quantum search with advice provides exactly that. We give such an adversary a cost model and a metric. For a device whose key has rank r, any quantum algorithm with classical access to the posteriors needs Omega(sqrt(r)) cipher evaluations, and block search achieves O(sqrt(r)); the per-instance advantage is exactly quadratic, and the super-quadratic exponents reported for search with advice are averages over the prior that apply to no single device. Under the NIST MAXDEPTH budget D and a Grover iteration of g gates and depth d, the quadratic advantage holds only for ranks up to (4D/(pi d))^2 and collapses to a constant factor beyond; with the best published AES-128 oracle and D = 2^40 the window closes near rank 2^58.6. We define the quantum-aware key rank, the classical rank of equal cost, computable from the rank estimators laboratories already run, and derive the classical rank a device must retain to keep a given threshold against each depth budget. Block search and amplitude amplification from the product-form posterior state are within a factor of two to four of each other on Hamming-weight posteriors, so the cost of coherent indexing decides between them. Experiments on simulated leakage and a toy cipher confirm the predicted window: at SNR 0.125 a depth-limited quantum adversary is worth about 22 traces to a classical one, however large its gate budget.

cs.CR / 28 / 2610.19335
Differentially Private Learning of Markov Chains: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity for Item and User Level Privacy
Devansh Gupta, Cristóbal Guzman, Enayat Ullah
stat.OT · cs.CR
Abstract
Sequential data such as documents, conversations, and trajectories are naturally partitioned across users, motivating privacy guarantees that protect each user's entire trajectory. We initiate the study of privately estimating the transition matrix of a discrete ergodic Markov chain from N independent trajectories of length T, with arbitrary initial distributions, under maximum row-wise ell 1 error. Besides N, T, and the number of states, our bounds depend on the minimum stationary probability and the pseudo-spectral gap, which govern state coverage and mixing. Under item-level privacy, we give upper and lower bounds that separate the costs of sampling, state occupancy and mixing, and privacy. Under user-level privacy, we reduce the problem for sufficiently long trajectories to private product distribution estimation. Along the way, we establish optimal user-level private bounds for estimating products of discrete distributions, which may be of independent interest. In the user level setting, our bounds are nearly tight in the large T regime, whereas in the item-level setting, our bounds as tight up-to a non-private term.
